analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans import cheaper prescription drugs from Canada without needing government approval first.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee never took up the bill, and it died without a single vote in the 108th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2003 law had authorized importing prescription drugs from Canada, but only if the Secretary of Health and Human Services first proved to Congress that the imports were safe and would save consumers money — a hurdle that kept the program from ever starting. This bill struck that requirement, ordered the Secretary to write the rules within a year, and required imported drugs to carry labels showing where they came from. In short, it would have opened a legal channel for Americans to buy medicines at Canada's lower prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who pay United States prices for brand-name prescription drugs, which are often far higher than the same drugs sell for in Canada. The bill would have let pharmacists and wholesalers import those drugs legally, creating price competition. It also created importing work for pharmacies and wholesale distributors.

how_it_helps.text: Repealed the federal requirement that the Secretary of Health and Human Services must first demonstrate to Congress that drug importation is safe and financially beneficial to consumers before the program could start [S2][S3].
Repealed the scheduled termination of the importation program, making it a standing rather than temporary authorization [S2].
Directed the Secretary to issue final rules for the importation program within one year of enactment, effective within 30 days after issuance [S2][S3].
Required imported drugs to be labeled with their country of origin and the names and addresses of the importer and exporter, giving consumers traceability [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose higher United States prices would face competition from cheaper Canadian imports, and indirectly the pharmacies and distributors that currently sell at the higher American prices. The government would bear the cost of writing and enforcing the new labeling and import rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill removed the condition that the Secretary of Health and Human Services must first certify to Congress that the imported products are safe and that consumers would actually benefit, meaning imports could begin without that official safety-and-savings finding [S2][S3].

By law the importation program was already conditioned on federal safety findings; critics of importation generally argue that foreign supply chains are harder to police against counterfeit or improperly stored medicines. The bill's labeling rules addressed traceability but left the safety question to the rulemaking process rather than a prior certification [S2][S3].
Consumer savings are not guaranteed: drug makers could restrict supply to Canada or raise prices there, and the bill itself does not estimate what Americans would save [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and well understood: the same medicines sell for less in Canada, and a legal importation channel would let Americans capture that difference. The honest cost is that the bill chose speed over caution — it stripped out the safety-and-savings certification rather than waiting for one, relying on labeling rules and later regulation to manage risk. A stronger version would have kept a safety review. Even allowing for that, the bill's promise to millions of Americans paying high drug prices outweighed its procedural shortcut.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee — and then in its Health subcommittee — for the rest of the 108th Congress, and no committee vote, floor vote, or hearing ever happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Marion Berry, a Democrat from Arkansas, introduced the bill on February 13, 2003, with 19 original cosponsors including one Republican, Rep. Jo Ann Emerson of Missouri [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
Two weeks later, on February 26, 2003, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Health, where it remained [S5].
The bill ended the Congress with 23 cosponsors — 21 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent — and no further committee or floor action [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the status quo: no legal importation channel competing with their United States prices. Consumers who buy prescription drugs got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept high prices

for.name: Rep. Marion Berry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Prescription Drug Price Reduction Act to start the Canadian drug importation program without prior federal certification.

for.name: 23 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, including Rep. Jo Ann Emerson (R-MO) among the original cosponsors and Rep. Bernie Sanders (I-VT).

for.name: AARP and consumer groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly pushed for legal drug importation from Canada during this period, a position widely covered at the time.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction, referred it to the Health subcommittee, and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote.

against.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that took no action on the bill; after leaving Congress he became the top lobbyist for the pharmaceutical industry's main trade group, PhRMA, in 2005.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers (PhRMA and its members)
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained campaign against drug importation legislation during the 108th Congress, including during the 2003 Medicare drug bill negotiations, arguing it posed safety risks and threatened research funding.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was 21 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent out of 23 — bipartisan in name but overwhelmingly Democratic — while the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Legal imports from Canada would compete with their high United States prices, which are the source of most industry profit. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against consumers seeking lower prices.
The bill would license them to import and resell Canadian drugs, creating a new line of business. Their gain comes from selling Americans cheaper medicine, so it runs with the public's interest.
The bill would open a regulated export channel to American customers, with labeling rules naming the exporter. Their gain depends on Americans accessing lower Canadian prices.
